top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: In collaboration with an information specialist, we developed a search strategy based on four search themes: 'opioid,' 'pain,' 'emergency,' and 'effectiveness' (detailed search strategies are available in Supplement Methods S1 ). The following databases were searched from their inception to May 5, 2022: CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and PsycINFO. An updated search was performed at the end of the process during the third week of January 2023 to collect recently published papers. We also searched Clini calTr ials.gov and the International Standard Randomized Controlled Trial Number registry for ongoing studies. Gray literature was searched using Google Scholar and the first 300 hits were screened to identify any relevant studies. References from studies meeting inclusion criteria were examined and their authors were contacted to identify additional relevant studies.

top_evidence.document_title: Efficacy of prescribed opioids for acute pain after being discharged from the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-­ analysis
top_evidence.text: This systematic review and meta-­ analysis was prospectively registered (PROSPERO CRD42022332009). Its results are presented as per the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-­ Analysis (PRISMA) guidelines (Data S1). 29 We also followed et al . the synthesis without meta-­ analysis reporting guidelines to complement the PRISMA guidelines. 30

top_evidence.section: Results > Search Results And Study Characteristics
top_evidence.text: The initial search strategy generated 5942 references after duplicate removal. Of these, 47 were kept for full-­ text review and seven studies were retained. One of them 36 was further removed since it used dextropropoxyphene, an opioid that has been withdrawn from the market in 2009 because of its association with lethal events. Therefore, six studies 37-­ 42 were finally included in this systematic review and meta-­ analysis (Figure 1 ). One study 39 compared two types of opioids (oxycodone and tramadol) to a placebo. Patients could consume rescue medications and placebo has demonstrated analgesic effects 43,44 ; we kept only the oxycodone versus placebo comparison as tramadol has nonopioid analgesic effects. 45 Another study 42 compared oxycodone to two nonopioids (NSAID and cyclobenzaprine); we kept only the oxycodone versus NSAIDs comparison since cyclobenzaprine is mainly a muscle relaxant. 46 One conflict on data extraction for the outcome measured in the study by Drendel et al. 40 was settled through consensus. Four differences in risk of bias assessment were observed between the two raters, two in the protection against contamination and two in the selective outcome reporting domain. These were resolved through consensus by the two raters. Four included studies 37,39,40,42 were conducted in the United States and two 38,41 in Canada; four studies 37-­ 39,42 included adult and two others 40,41 included pediatric populations (Table 1 ). All studies included patients with musculoskeletal pain; five of them 37,38,40-­ 42 had NSAIDs as a comparator and one had a placebo. 39 Three studies 37,38,40 used codeine as the opioid, and the three others used hydrocodone, 39 morphine, 41 or oxycodone. 42 Except for morphine, opioids were combined with acetaminophen and their dosage and administration frequency were not equivalent. The type of NSAIDs used also varied across studies: diflunisal, ketorolac, ibuprofen (two studies), and naproxen. Follow-­ up duration varied from 1 to 7 days and outcomes were pain relief for five studies 37-­ 39,41,42 and treatment failure (use of rescue medication) for the other. 40 The majority of studies applied extensive exclusion criteria (Supplement Table S2 ). top_evidence.text: Identified references from all databases were transferred to Covidence systematic review manager (Covidence systematic review software, Veritas Health Innovation, available at www.covid ence.org). Eight reviewers (RD, JP, MM, DW, GF, AF, AO, and AC) participated in a two-­ stage selection process of eligible studies. After duplicate removal, each citation was screened by two independent reviewers using the title and abstract for potential relevance. The full text of the remaining citations was then independently evaluated by two reviewers against inclusion and exclusion criteria. During both stages, a third reviewer (RD or AC) resolved discrepancies.
